## Where the ladder turns into a circle

Timbre steps aside now. Pitch is the only thing moving in this lesson, and it
carries two locations at once. MIDI note 60 is one particular C at one
particular height. The letter C also ties that note to every other C on the
instrument, above and below it. Keep the height and you have an address. Drop
the height and you have a family.

Walk from 60 up to 72 one semitone at a time and you'll hear both at once.
Thirteen notes, twelve rises, and the last one is recognisably the first again
in a higher place. A *pitch class* is your position in that repeating
twelve-step cycle once the octave has been thrown away. In code it's `pitch %
12`. Notes 36, 60 and 84 are three separate addresses and a single pitch class:
0.

Your keyboard already draws the cycle. Black keys come in a group of two and a
group of three, and those groups change nothing about the spacing, since every
step is still one semitone. What they give you is a place marker. Before you
press Run, look at the second half of the program and predict this: which of
the two passes covers more musical distance, and which one plays more notes?

## Climb twelve, then filter for one

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 120
use_synth :piano

define :pitch_class do |pitch|
  pitch % 12
end

(60..72).each do |pitch|
  play pitch, release: 0.15
  puts "pitch #{pitch}, class #{pitch_class(pitch)}"
  sleep 0.25
end

sleep 1
(36..84).select { |pitch| pitch_class(pitch) == 0 }.each do |pitch|
  play pitch, release: 0.4
  sleep 0.5
end
```

The first pass climbs through all twelve classes and lands back on class 0 at
note 72. Keep the log in view while it runs. Class counts 0 to 11, wraps to 0,
and starts again, while the MIDI address underneath it climbs without a break.
The second pass sweeps four octaves and keeps only class 0, so you get widely
separated Cs, each one twelve semitones above the last.

## Rotate the cycle

1. Change the selected class from `0` to `7` and the second pass finds every G
   in range. New addresses, identical spacing: twelve semitones from each
   result to the next.

2. Restore class 0, then start the chromatic walk at 61. The printed classes
   now begin at 1 and return to 1 at note 73. You rotated the cycle without
   changing its length or its direction.

3. Restore the original range and stretch each chromatic sleep to `0.5`. Trace
   the notes on a keyboard diagram or a controller as they sound. At the slower
   rate the black-key groups have time to register as landmarks.

## What modulo keeps and what it throws away

Modulo folds an integer address onto a repeating range. Divide a MIDI note by
twelve and the remainder lands somewhere from 0 to 11; any two notes twelve
apart share it. You already know the shape from a ring buffer or a clock face.
The count keeps rising, the position keeps coming round.

That reduction earns its place because plenty of musical questions ignore
height entirely. A chord analyser wants to know that some voice is supplying
class 0, whichever C the player reached for. Transposition adds a fixed amount
and takes the remainder to stay inside the class set.

The loss matters just as much. Once 48, 60 and 72 have all become 0, nothing
downstream can recover which one you started from. You can't play a pitch
class. Somebody has to choose a register first. So keep the full address
whenever range, voicing, or actual frequency is still part of the question.

C sits at class 0 because C4 is MIDI 60, and `60 % 12` is 0. Other systems
display names instead of integers, or start counting somewhere else entirely.
Twelve positions either way. Fix the convention at the boundary of your
program, compare plain integers inside it, and attach a display name at the
point where a person reads the output.

Printing both coordinates together separates two failures that sound alike. If
the notes reach an octave but the class never wraps, your modulo is wrong. If
the class wraps correctly but playback lands in the wrong octave, you used a
class somewhere an address belonged.

Lesson 9 makes register the variable under study, so it holds on to complete
MIDI addresses. Lesson 10 adds a second thing modulo erases: two spellings that
share one sounding class while describing different musical motion.

## Build yourself a chromatic browser

Write a browser with variables named `start` and `offset`. For offsets 0
through 12, play `start + offset` and print the full MIDI address next to its
pitch class. Thirteen rows, one complete cycle, first and last sharing a class.

Then add a second pass that searches MIDI 36 through 84 for one class you
choose, printing each address before it plays. Check the arithmetic in the log,
then audition both passes in Sonic Pi 5. The browser should move by semitone
and the filtered notes by octave. Two sounds that different, from two views of
the same integers.
